history.heading: Ancient Egypt
paragraphs: Egypt is home to one of the world's oldest civilisations, which developed along the Nile. Around 3100 BCE, Upper and Lower Egypt were unified under the first pharaohs. During the Old Kingdom, the pyramids of Giza were built; the Great Pyramid is the only surviving wonder of the ancient world.

Over nearly three thousand years, Egypt developed hieroglyphic writing, monumental temples at Karnak and Luxor, advanced mathematics and medicine, and a rich religion focused on the afterlife. The New Kingdom pharaohs, such as Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II, ruled an empire stretching into the Levant and Nubia.

history.heading: Greeks, Romans and Arabs
paragraphs: Alexander the Great conquered Egypt in 332 BCE, and the Ptolemaic dynasty ruled from Alexandria, home of the famous Library and Lighthouse. After Cleopatra VII's death in 30 BCE, Egypt became a Roman province and the empire's breadbasket. Christianity spread early, and the Coptic Church was founded.

Arab armies conquered Egypt in 641, bringing Islam and the Arabic language. Cairo was founded by the Fatimids in 969 and became a great centre of Islamic civilisation, with Al-Azhar University. Saladin, the Mamluks and, from 1517, the Ottomans ruled Egypt.

history.heading: Modern Egypt
paragraphs: Napoleon invaded in 1798. Muhammad Ali, who took power in 1805, modernised the army and economy. The Suez Canal opened in 1869, and Britain occupied Egypt in 1882. Egypt became formally independent in 1922 as a kingdom, though British influence remained.

In 1952 the Free Officers overthrew the monarchy. Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in 1956, became a leader of Arab nationalism and built the Aswan High Dam. Egypt fought wars with Israel in 1948, 1956, 1967 and 1973. Anwar Sadat signed a peace treaty with Israel in 1979 and was assassinated in 1981. Hosni Mubarak ruled for 30 years.

history.heading: Revolution and after
paragraphs: Mass protests in Tahrir Square during the Arab Spring forced Mubarak to resign in 2011. Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood was elected president in 2012 but was removed by the military in 2013 after mass protests. Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, the army chief, became president in 2014.

culture.heading: Language and religion
paragraphs: Arabic is the official language, and Egyptian Arabic is widely understood across the Arab world thanks to Egyptian films and television. Most Egyptians are Sunni Muslim, and Coptic Christians form the largest Christian community in the Middle East.
Al-Azhar in Cairo is one of the most important institutions of Sunni Islamic learning.

culture.heading: Arts and entertainment
paragraphs: Egypt has long been a cultural centre of the Arab world. Naguib Mahfouz won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1988. Umm Kulthum is considered one of the greatest Arab singers, and Egypt's film industry, sometimes called the "Hollywood of the Middle East", has been highly influential.
The Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids, one of the largest archaeological museums in the world, fully opened in 2025.

culture.heading: Food and daily life
paragraphs: Egyptian food includes koshari (lentils, rice and pasta with tomato sauce), ful medames (fava beans), ta'ameya (falafel) and molokhia. Tea and coffee houses are social hubs.
Football is the most popular sport; Al Ahly and Zamalek are among Africa's most successful clubs, and Mohamed Salah is a national hero.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Egypt is a presidential republic in which the president holds strong powers and the military plays a central role in politics and the economy. Constitutional amendments in 2019 extended presidential terms. Human rights groups report widespread restrictions on opposition, media and civil society, and large numbers of political prisoners.

politics.heading: Regional power
paragraphs: Egypt is the most populous Arab country and a key regional actor. It hosts the Arab League headquarters, mediates in Israeli-Palestinian conflicts, including over Gaza, and receives significant US military aid. A dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Nile, on which Egypt depends for almost all its water, is a major concern.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Egypt has one of the largest economies in Africa. Key sources of income are tourism, Suez Canal fees, remittances from Egyptians abroad, natural gas, and exports of petroleum products, chemicals, textiles and agricultural goods such as cotton and citrus. Most of the population lives along the Nile Valley and Delta, on a small fraction of the country's land.
The government has invested heavily in megaprojects, including a new administrative capital east of Cairo.

economy.heading: Challenges
paragraphs: Egypt faces high public debt, high inflation, a rapidly growing population and foreign currency shortages. The Egyptian pound has been devalued several times. Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea from late 2023 sharply reduced Suez Canal revenues. In 2024 a large investment deal with the UAE and an expanded IMF programme provided support.
